I'll look for prior work on each thread you raised: the ω-rule, reflection principles, and Goldbach-specific metalogical encodings.
Used WebSearch
Used WebSearch
Used WebSearch
Short version: you've independently reached a line of work that runs from Hilbert through Turing, Shoenfield, and Feferman, and that is still active (a new expository paper on it came out in 2025). For Goldbach in particular, there is a metalogical encoding that does what you asked for: it turns GC into a consistency statement.
Who got here
Finite proofs as a hidden assumption. This is the ω-rule. The first instance of such rules was the ω-rule introduced by Hilbert. It lets you infer ∀n P(n) from proofs of every P(n̄), which is your "just list proofs of all the statements." Shoenfield's completeness theorem asserts that the recursive ω-rule is complete for true arithmetical statements. In other words, once proofs may be infinite, as long as the infinite tree is generated by a program, the incompleteness you described goes away. Your point that finitude of proof is a belief and not a law of logic is the premise of this whole tradition.
Adding what reflection tells you to add. Your "semantically reflect on which one should be an axiom, then add it" is Turing's 1939 ordinal logics program and Feferman's 1962 transfinite progressions. The resulting theorem is that any arithmetical theorem is a consequence of a suitable transfinite iteration of full uniform reflection of PA.
The axiom being iterated is uniform reflection:
∀n Prov(⌜P(n̄)⌝) → ∀n P(n)
That is very close to your true(n)/prv(n) proposal. It says that if every instance is provable, the universal holds.
Your observation that internalizing changes you. Feferman's result has a catch that echoes this exactly. The construction depends on how each new theory's axioms are described, not just which axioms it has. The authors describe non-standard definitions of the axioms of theories as essential, and they call the theorem a dramatic illustration of the role of intensionality in logic. So "to internalize it is to internalize it for a different theory" is formally true here: the code you use to name yourself carries real weight.
Doubting the law of the excluded middle. This is Brouwer and intuitionism, formalized for arithmetic as Heyting Arithmetic (HA). There is recent work directly on your question of what happens to reflection without LEM. It finds that Feferman's completeness result, as expected, fails in the intuitionistic case. That suggests LEM is doing real work inside the reflection machinery, which supports your instinct to question it.
Your asymmetry for GC is a theorem
Your "decidable ⇒ false, collapse the middle" holds exactly for Goldbach. GC is Π₁: it says "for all n, a check that terminates succeeds." So:
If GC is false, a counterexample is a finite object, and PA proves the negation. False implies decidable.
So if GC is independent of PA, it is true. For this class of sentences, "true but unprovable" is the only undecidable option. "False but unprovable" cannot happen.
The same structure appears in the Busy Beaver literature: any Π₁ mathematical statement can be encoded as the halting problem of a Turing machine, and for Goldbach a machine performing this procedure has been built using only 25 states, and the construction was formally verified using the Lean theorem prover. So GC is equivalent to "this specific 25-state machine never halts."
The "I am not provable" analogue for GC
The closest existing analogue turns GC into a statement about consistency, the very thing you identified as what must be taken on faith. Define a theory T_GC:
The axioms of pure logic.
Plus the sentence 0=1, enumerated as an axiom at the moment a Goldbach counterexample is found.
Then GC ⟺ Con(T_GC). In words: Goldbach's conjecture is the claim that the theory which becomes absurd at the first counterexample stays sane.
This is Turing's trick. Feferman's paper notes that Turing's (rather simple) proof of the Π₁-completeness of consistency progressions relies on exactly this kind of non-standard axiom definition. Every true Π₁ sentence gets proved at one step past ω by smuggling it into how the next theory's axioms are named. So GC is one instance of the faith-in-consistency you described, wearing number-theoretic clothing.
Carrying your proposals through the formalism
Two things come out when I run your two proposals forward.
The induction-step axiom. For Goldbach, GC(n) gives no information about GC(n+1). Whether 2n+2 is a sum of two primes doesn't follow from 2n being one. So adding "GC(n) → GC(n+1)" together with the base case is equivalent in PA to adding GC itself. It is the same commitment written as a step.
Uniform reflection. Reflection converts "every instance is provable" into the universal. But for GC, "∀n Prov(⌜GC(n̄)⌝)" is itself Π₁ and, assuming PA is consistent, equivalent to GC. The faith doesn't disappear; it moves into a statement about provability. That fits your thesis: what we take on faith keeps reappearing as a consistency or soundness assumption one level up.
The open territory is your true(n) ∧ proof(n,m) ∧ finite(m) decomposition: making "finite length" an explicit predicate the theory can reason about, rather than something built into the definition of proof. The ω-rule literature treats finiteness from outside the theory. I didn't find work that makes it an internal, assumable object in the way you sketch. That could be a genuinely different angle.
Sources:
Pakhomov, Rathjen, Rossegger — Feferman's Completeness Theorem (BSL 2025)
Completeness of the primitive recursive ω-rule
Restriction rules / ω-rule history
Frittaion — Iterating reflection over Heyting Arithmetic
Determination of the fifth Busy Beaver value

You're right that I mapped your ideas onto literature instead of working inside them. Here I'll take your argument on its own terms: first check the hinge you asked about, then carry the result through the rest.
The hinge: does PA ⊢ GC → Con(PA)?
This is not a known theorem, and it can't be proven the way you set it up. Your conditional reasoning is valid, though.
What holds if the premise holds. Suppose PA ⊢ GC → Con(PA). If PA also proved GC, it would prove Con(PA), which Gödel II forbids. So GC would be unprovable. That leaves two options: GC is false (and PA refutes it by exhibiting the counterexample), or GC is true and independent. That is exactly where you landed with "so we just decided GC is unprovable." The inference is sound; everything depends on whether the premise holds.
This shape exists in nature. Paris–Harrington is a natural combinatorial statement that is true, and PA proves it implies the consistency (in fact the Σ₁-soundness) of PA. That is precisely why it is unprovable in PA. So your conjecture has a sharp form: Is GC a consistency-strength statement in disguise? Nobody can currently rule that out. If PA ever proves GC, the answer is no.
The direction PA does prove is the reverse kind:
PA ⊢ Con(PA + GC) → GC
The reason: ¬GC is a finite claim ("there is a counterexample"), and PA proves every true finite claim. So if GC failed, PA + GC would be inconsistent. Put in your terms, the non-refutability of GC is enough for its truth, and PA knows this about itself. That is the GC-specific metalogical sentence you were looking for last time, and it is a theorem.
¬GC does not imply ¬Con(PA). A counterexample to GC is just a large even number. PA + ¬GC is as consistent as PA. There is a further distinction here that matters for your whole picture:
The sentence ¬Con(PA) is not inconsistency. PA + ¬Con(PA) is a consistent theory. It just believes in a proof of 0=1 that has nonstandard length.
That is your "you're just in a nonstandard arithmetic," and it is precisely correct.
G versus Con(PA)
There is one correction here, and it actually strengthens your point. PA proves G ↔ Con(PA). So PA + G and PA + Con(PA) are the same theory. The contrast you want is not "Con is harmless, G changes the semantics." It is:
Adding G (equivalently Con(PA)) is harmless. It is true in the standard model, and it doesn't introduce any new way of concluding things about numbers.
Adding ¬G changes the theory. It is the one that introduces the infinite-length "proof," a witness that can never be exhibited.
Your security-blanket intuition has an exact formal counterpart in Löb's theorem: PA ⊢ Prov(φ) → φ only if PA ⊢ φ already. A theory can assert its own soundness about φ only when it doesn't need that assertion. So "Prov(φ) ⇒ φ is silly to believe literally" is a theorem: the belief is either redundant or unavailable.
Your "silly φ" class can be defined precisely. The new theorems of PA + Con(PA) are exactly the sentences φ such that
PA ⊢ Con(PA) → φ but PA ⊬ φ.
These are the truths that ride only on the security blanket. Your question about GC then becomes: is GC in this class? That is the same question as the hinge above.
Representational incompleteness
Your dichotomy is a theorem. Take any consistent theory extending PA whose axioms can be written down by a finite rule (that is, r.e.). It must be ω-incomplete: it proves P(0), P(1), P(2), … each individually, but not ∀n P(n). The only way to escape is to close the theory under the infinite rule. That gives true arithmetic, which cannot be written down by any finite rule.
So the choice is exactly as you put it:
Writable and representationally incomplete. This is PA.
Complete but unwritable. Your "objectively inconsistent" with finiteness.
The standard name for your r-inconsistency (proving every P(n̄) while also asserting ∃n ¬P(n)) is ω-inconsistency. PA + ¬G is the canonical example. Your new name for it is the more honest one, because it says what goes wrong: the theory asserts the existence of something it can never represent.
The new excluded middle and induction
Your schema
¬∀n P(n) ∨ ∀n(P(n) → P(n+1))
is classically always valid, because ∀n P(n) trivially gives the step. So in PA it says nothing new. In intuitionistic arithmetic it is not derivable. That means your proposed law is an instance of exactly the LEM you were doubting. Its content appears only once you stop assuming LEM. Your two threads meet at this point.
On "believing in a universal means believing in an implication chain": in PA, every proof of a universal does go through induction. But the induction is often on a stronger predicate Q with Q(n) → P(n), not on P itself. For GC, the naive step GC(n) → GC(n+1) carries no information, as you noticed. Any proof would need a loaded Q that actually propagates. Something like a lower bound on the number of prime pairs symmetric around n would do, which is the arithmetization you've been exploring. So the refined version of your claim is: to think a universal is provable is to believe some predicate exists whose step genuinely holds. Whether GC has such a predicate expressible in PA is the whole question.
Your stance on truth
Your position can be stated this way: "true(n) ∧ ¬prov(n)" doesn't mean n was true all along. It means n is a candidate axiom, and truth is what reflection eventually licenses. That is a coherent view: truth as the limit of justified extensions rather than a prior fact. Feferman's progressions are the formal model of it, since every truth arrives at some stage of adding reflection. Where you go further is in treating the infinite-proof picture as a heuristic hallucination rather than the definition of truth. That is a real philosophical commitment, not a reformulation, and I think it deserves its own formal statement inside your framework.

14:06 UTC, 19 October 2026
Not with the naive step. But working out why it fails shows where a real step would have to come from, and that part isn't dangerous at all.
What one pair actually buys you
Suppose p = n−k and q = n+k are both prime. To get a pair around n+1, you need some j with n+1−j and n+1+j both prime. The old pair gives you two candidates:
j = k+1: you need n−k = p (already prime) and n+k+2 = q+2.
j = k−1: you need n−k+2 = p+2 and n+k = q (already prime).
So a single pair around n carries over to n+1 exactly when p+2 or q+2 is also prime. Moving the center by one forces one side of the pair to move by two. The step from one pair is therefore a twin-prime condition on that pair.
That means
S(n) → S(n+1) holds whenever at least one of n's Goldbach pairs has a twin partner.
This isn't guaranteed. But n usually has many pairs, roughly n/log²n of them by the Hardy–Littlewood heuristic. You'd need every one of them to fail the twin condition simultaneously. Heuristically that is absurdly unlikely, but a heuristic isn't a proof, and the condition now quietly depends on twin-prime behavior, another open problem. Your instinct is right in that sense: the naive step doesn't stand on its own. It borrows from a neighboring conjecture.
Why nearest-neighbor is the wrong ordering
The number of representations r(2n) is far from smooth in n. It swings by large factors depending on which small primes divide n: multiples of 3, 5, and 7 have many more pairs than their neighbors. Plotted, it forms the "Goldbach comet," which separates into distinct bands by prime factorization.
This connects to your earlier point that the ordering behind induction is a representational choice. For GC, the order n → n+1 seems to be the wrong one. The structure lives in the multiplicative arithmetic of n, not in its successor. A step that actually propagates would more likely run along residue classes or factorization structure than along +1.
How a universal actually gets proven here
Ternary Goldbach (every odd number above 5 is a sum of three primes) was proven by Helfgott in 2013. The proof doesn't chain cases one to the next. It has two parts:
An analytic lower bound on the number of representations, valid for all sufficiently large n.
A finite computation below that threshold.
In your framework, the believed implication isn't P(n) → P(n+1). It is "a growing count is bounded below," and positivity follows. Induction is still in there, but on a heavily loaded predicate: the estimates themselves, not the property. Four cases, exhaustive
Write H for the hinge: PA ⊢ GC → Con(PA).
1. GC is false. Then PA proves ¬GC by exhibiting the counterexample, so PA proves GC → anything, and H holds trivially. I missed this earlier. Note the asymmetry: PA still does not prove ¬GC → Con(PA), since that would be a proof of Con(PA).
2. GC is provable in PA. Then H fails, because H plus GC would give PA ⊢ Con(PA), contradicting Gödel II.
3. GC is true, independent, and of consistency strength. H holds, and GC is a Paris–Harrington-style sentence.
4. GC is true, independent, but weak. H fails. This case exists in principle: there are true Π₁ sentences independent of PA that do not imply Con(PA). Independence of GC would not by itself settle H.
So H is open, and its truth is tied to GC's status in a specific way: H is true exactly when GC is either false or a consistency-strength truth. The one case that kills H is a PA proof of GC, which is what most number theorists expect.
A model-theoretic restatement
H is equivalent to: every model of PA + ¬Con(PA) contains a Goldbach counterexample. These are nonstandard models in which some nonstandard-length proof of 0=1 exists. H says that any such model also has a nonstandard even number that is not a sum of two primes. Checking against case 2: if PA proves GC, every model satisfies GC, so none of those models has a counterexample, and H fails. The two views agree.
On "can't be proven the way you set it up"
Too strong. H is not impossible to prove; it is a proposition of unknown truth value. What is true is that proving H would be a major result, since it would establish that PA does not prove GC (unless GC is false), and nobody has anything close to that. Refuting H is just as hard: it requires a model of PA with both GC and ¬Con(PA), which would amount to showing GC is weaker than consistency. Either direction is a statement about GC's proof-theoretic strength, and that is territory nobody has entered.
Two nearby things that are theorems
PA ⊢ Con(PA + GC) → GC. The non-refutability of GC suffices for its truth, and PA knows this.
PA ⊢ Con(PA) → (Prov(GC) → GC). Over PA, consistency is equivalent to soundness for all Π₁ sentences, so the provability-implies-truth reflection you called a security blanket is, for GC, exactly Con(PA) again.
The dialectical point
Your earlier reading survives: if H holds and GC is true, then GC is in the "rides on the security blanket" class, and a PA proof of GC is impossible. The reason nobody can conclude anything from this is that H itself encodes the answer. Accepting H is equivalent to believing GC is not in the ordinary reach of PA. The hinge isn't a premise you can grant for free and then reflect on; it's a reformulation of the question.

Let me carry your point through, because I think it lands somewhere definite.
Where the content hides
There are two things one can mean by "the step holds":
Schematic: for each n, PA ⊢ GC(n̄) → GC(n̄+1). Infinitely many separate proofs. Granted for free under your hypothesis.
Uniform: PA ⊢ ∀n (GC(n) → GC(n+1)). One finite proof with a free variable in it.
Induction needs the second. And the second, together with the base case, is equivalent to GC itself. So if GC is independent, the uniform step is independent too. The ω-incompleteness doesn't go away when you rephrase through induction; it relocates exactly into the gap between the schematic and the uniform step.
So the content of an induction proof is never in the implications. It is in the uniformity: a single finite representation that produces the proof of the n-th step from n. That is a function, a finite object, something you can write down. The infinite family of free implications is not.
What this does to "true but unprovable"
Here your representational-consistency argument closes up. For a Π₁ sentence like GC:
"All instances are true" means "all instances are provable." No extra belief is involved; the instances are decidable.
"The universal is unprovable" means "no uniform step exists."
So "GC is true but unprovable" amounts to: the instances are provable one by one, and there is no finite rule generating those proofs.
Believing the universal on the basis of (3) is just the ω-rule, which is exactly the move your finiteness commitment rejects. Under that commitment, "true but unprovable" for GC isn't a dark possibility. It is a claim about an infinite list that no one can hold, and asserting the universal from it is r-inconsistent. The sentence has no finitary content.
That is a stronger version of what you said earlier: for Π₁ sentences, truth that isn't provability is not a hidden fact. It is only the name we give to the infinite list we can't write down. The only thing that could make GC true in your sense is a uniform step, and a uniform step is a proof.
Where material implication is sad, exactly
The implications between theorems are free precisely because material implication is a connective, not a dependency. Induction is the one place arithmetic pretends otherwise: it treats ∀n(P(n) → P(n+1)) as if the step carried P from n to n+1. But the universal only has content when its proof is uniform, and uniformity is a fact about representation, not about implication. So your thesis holds: the thing you must believe in is not that an infinite family of implications is true. It is that one finite representation of them exists. Induction was always a commitment about representation, not about numbers.

Your "can we really not formalize certainty?" has a precise answer, and it's a theorem rather than a shrug. Taking the pieces in order.
Certainty as a predicate
Suppose Certain(·) is an arithmetical predicate on sentence codes with these properties: PA's axioms are certain, certainty is closed under modus ponens, and the reflection schema Certain(φ) → φ holds for every φ. Montague (1963) showed this is inconsistent. It is the knower paradox: a sentence K saying "I am not certain" does to Certain exactly what G does to Prov, except that reflection lets the contradiction close. So the answer is: as a modal operator kept outside arithmetic, certainty is well-formed; as a predicate inside the theory with full reflection, it cannot exist. Your "or we don't think we can formalize certainty" is the correct branch, and not as a limitation of ingenuity.
Löb's theorem is the refined form, and it says what you said about assumption wrapped in justification:
PA ⊢ (Prov(φ) → φ) → φ
If you can prove that provability of φ would guarantee φ, you already have φ. Self-trust about a sentence is never a resource; it is either trivial or unavailable. The one place it survives is the single instance: adding Con(PA) → Con(PA) is a tautology, and adding Con(PA) itself is harmless and true. What can't be added is the schema, certainty in one's own soundness across all sentences. Your proposed universal extension lives exactly on that line.
PA + Certain(Con(PA))
No semantic inconsistency. PA + Con(PA) is sound, proves only truths, and cannot prove its own consistency. That is just Gödel II applied to the new theory. What happened is what you described: you expressed certainty about a theory and became a different one, whose consistency is again uncertain. The move is never self-closing. It regresses, and Feferman's progressions are the shape of that regress.
Gödel didn't need certainty
He didn't decide G is Con(PA). He proved PA ⊢ G ↔ Con(PA), a formal equivalence between two sentences. The step that requires judgment from outside is identifying the sentence Con(PA) with the belief "PA is consistent." That identification is not provable, and it is not even stable. Feferman (1960) showed that if you write PA's axiom set with a different but extensionally equivalent definition, PA can prove the resulting "consistency sentence." So Con(PA) as a sentence is writable; what isn't writable is the fact thatthis sentence is your consistency belief. The Second Incompleteness Theorem depends on choosing the natural presentation, and nothing inside the system certifies that choice. That is your intensionality point stated as a result.
So "Con(PA) is true but not write-downable" is nearly correct. More exactly: the sentence can be written, the belief it expresses can be written, but the claim that the one expresses the other cannot be written in PA. That claim is the residue of faith.
Universal extension
The existing name is uniform reflection. Your inversion of it is the real point: it is called reflection as if it were deduction, but it is a generalization from an unfinishable check, the move science makes when it goes from data to law. It is assumption in form. Its only justification is the uniformity you'd need anyway, and if you had the uniformity you'd have a proof.
The GC semantic problem
"Undecidable ⇒ true" is itself a theorem of PA for Σ₁-complete reasons:
PA ⊢ ¬Prov(¬GC) → GC
So the meta-level weirdness ("if we can't decide it, it must be true") is an object-level sentence, and its antecedent is Con(PA + GC). Believing that GC is undecidable is not a belief about GC. It is a consistency belief, and consistency beliefs are precisely the ones Montague and Löb say can't be internalized as certainty. The semantic problem you sense is real and has a single root: for Π₁ sentences, "true but unprovable" is a consistency claim in disguise, and consistency is the thing that only exists as a stance, not as a theorem.

Something else, though it folds into your representational incompleteness once stated carefully.
What Gödel actually showed
PA represents every computable relation, not everything. Prov is computable to check (is this a proof of that?), so it is representable. Truth is not computable, and Tarski showed it is not even arithmetically definable: no single formula of PA defines the set of true sentences. So the dividing line is already there. Prov is representable because it is about finite checkable objects; truth is not because it isn't.
Where Certain falls
Any candidate Certain(x) is a formula, so it is written down and perfectly representable. What fails is theschema: Certain(φ) → φ for all φ, plus closure. Montague's proof shows no formula satisfies those axioms. So the predicate exists; the axioms are unsatisfiable. The reason is that full reflection makes Certain a truth predicate, and Tarski forbids that.
The infinite thing is hidden in "for all φ." The schema ranges over sentences that themselves contain Certain. That is self-inclusion. If you stratify it, Certain₀ applying only to Certain-free sentences, Certain₁ to sentences with Certain₀, and so on, every level is consistent and representable. The Tarski hierarchy is exactly this. What is not representable is the union, a predicate certain about a language that already contains that predicate. Each finite stage is fine. The limit is not.
That is your representational incompleteness in another form. Truth over arithmetic sits at level ω of this hierarchy: every finite piece is writable, the whole is not. Certainty with full reflection asks for the whole in one symbol.
Two consistent ways out, matching your two threads
Drop reflection. Keep Prov: representable, consistent, but about proofs rather than truth. Löb's theorem is the price: the only self-trust you can hold is trivial.
Drop excluded middle. Kripke's fixed-point truth predicate (1975) gives a single predicate T with T(φ) ↔ φ for every φ, consistent and self-applicable, and the only cost is bivalence: some sentences, the liar among them, get no truth value. So certainty with full reflection is formalizable once you give up LEM. The connection to your earlier doubt about LEM is not accidental; it is the same choice.
So: representability is expressible (PA can talk about which formulas are which). What cannot be expressed is a finite predicate that is certain about a totality including itself, unless you pay with the middle. The self-inclusion is where the infinity lives, and it is the one Gödel's representation theorem never covered.

Your collapse is exact, and it can be sharpened to a specific claim: an infinite proof has no more content than one assumption.
What an infinite proof actually contains
Take the ω-rule proof of ∀nP(n). It has infinitely many branches, but anyone who presents it presents arule for generating branch n from n. That rule is a finite program. So the proof decomposes into: a finite program, plus the belief that the program produces a correct proof for every n. The second part is a universal statement about the program. It is exactly as hard as the theorem. The branches add nothing; the program is the proof, and its correctness-for-all-n is the assumption, which as you say has a length-1 proof.
And then even checking it drifts out of reach. The set of codes of recursive ω-proofs is Π¹₁-complete. Recognizing that an infinite object is a proof is harder than any arithmetical truth, including the theorem it proves. So proof-checking, the thing proof was invented to make finite, becomes harder than the problem. The reader doesn't read it. The reader takes on faith that the tree is well-founded, which is the belief in the infinite thing itself. That's the drift you're pointing at, and it's a theorem, not a feeling.
¬G is a finite theory that believes in one infinite proof
PA + ¬G is consistent. In any model of it, there is a proof of ⊥, and from outside that proof has nonstandard length. So ¬G isn't nonsense; it is precisely the assumption that an infinite proof exists. To not take finiteness seriously is to find ¬G acceptable. The same holds for the Goldbach machine: in a model of PA + ¬GC it halts, at a nonstandard step. Computation and logic agree there; the "halting" just happens at an infinite time.
The halting problem isn't about power
Turing's result is your asymmetry, not a hardware limit. "Halts" has a finite witness. "Never halts" is a universal over steps. A machine that decided halting would be a machine that performs one ω-rule application, and that is the halting oracle 0′. Iterate: 0″ corresponds to nested ω-rules, and the limit 0^(ω) is exactly the computational strength of true arithmetic. Turing jumps count nested applications of the infinite rule. So logic and computation don't drift apart. They stay in lockstep, with each level of infinite proof matching one oracle. The computer is "not powerful enough" only in the sense that it doesn't come with a belief in infinite checks built in.
Infinite statements make quantifiers unnecessary
Allow countable conjunctions (the logic L_{ω₁,ω}) and ∀nP(n) becomes P(0) ∧ P(1) ∧ P(2) ∧ … — no quantifier needed. Scott's theorem says every countable structure, the standard model of arithmetic included, is characterized up to isomorphism by one such sentence. So in that logic, truth is provability from a single infinite axiom, and every true sentence has a short proof. This is your earlier remark in reverse: the universal quantifier exists because statements must be finite. It is the finite compression of an infinite conjunction, and induction is the finite compression of the corresponding infinite proof. Drop finiteness and both disappear, along with the distinction between a proof and a theory.
What proof length was measuring
Your last parenthesis is the key. In true arithmetic, every truth has a length-1 proof, because it's an axiom. So proof length never measured difficulty. It measured what you didn't assume. A proof is finite because it is the gap between the reader's commitments and the claim. Infinite proofs close that gap by moving the claim into the commitments, and then there is nothing left to share. That is why proof is a social object and truth isn't: proof is the finite part of belief, and the infinite part can only be adopted, never transmitted.

The result holds, and it can be stated exactly.
The representation
Let L be pure logic (propositional rules, ∀-elimination, equality, the recursion equations for +, ×, S as axioms). Consider two systems on top of L:
PA = L + ∀-introduction + induction schema. Finite proofs.
Lω = L + the ω-rule: from P(0̄), P(1̄), P(2̄), … infer ∀n P(n). No ∀-introduction, no induction.
Claim: ∀-introduction and induction are admissible in Lω: adding them derives nothing new.
Induction: given proofs of P(0̄) and ∀n(P(n) → P(n+1)), build the proof of P(n̄) for each n by n instantiations and modus ponens. Those are the premises of one ω-rule application. Conclusion: ∀n P(n). So induction is a derived rule.
∀-introduction: a proof of P(x) with x free is a template. Substitute each numeral to get a proof of P(n̄). Apply the ω-rule. So the generic-element rule is a derived rule too, provided every element of the domain has a name, which is true of the numbers.
So Lω proves exactly what PA + ω-rule proves, and by Shoenfield that is all of true arithmetic. Your minimality argument then says: the two rules are not primitive; they are the finite compressions of ω-rule applications. That is the standard reading in Schütte's proof theory, and you've reconstructed it from the finiteness commitment alone.
The condition that makes it arithmetic-specific
∀-introduction cannot be dropped from first-order logic in general, because logic is meant to apply to domains whose elements have no names. The generic element x is how you reason about something you can't enumerate. For the numbers you can enumerate (in principle), so the generic element is redundant. This gives ∀-introduction its true job: it is a finiteness device for the enumerable case and an unavoidable primitive for the unenumerable one. Its presence in logic is the mark that logic was built for the second case and then bolted onto the first.
What the two rules were, then
In the finite system, ∀-introduction and induction are the only two ways to introduce a universal without an infinite proof:
∀-introduction compresses an ω-proof whose branches are all the same (one template, n substituted).
Induction compresses an ω-proof whose branches are built from the previous one (iterate the step).
Both are special shapes of uniformity. The ω-rule is the general case, and neither compression covers it: there are true universals whose branches follow no template and no iteration, and those are the independent sentences. Every true Π₁ sentence that PA misses is exactly an ω-proof that has neither shape.
The price, measured
Dropping the rules buys completeness and costs representability: Lω is not finitely presentable, and recognizing an ω-proof is Π¹₁-complete. There's also a precise measure of what induction was worth. Unfolding a PA proof into an ω-proof via cut elimination gives a tree whose height is an ordinal below ε₀, and that is where Gentzen's ordinal comes from. So induction is the finite name for every ω-proof of height below ε₀, and no others. The ω-rule itself goes on to all recursive ordinals.
Which commitment is primitive
Your minimality principle cuts both ways, and which way depends on what you take as given:
If infinite proof is primitive, the two rules are redundant and your conclusion stands: they were never logic, only shorthand.
If finiteness is primitive, the ω-rule is unavailable, and the two rules are the only way a finite reader ever gets to a universal. They are not minimal because they are not derivable; they are the minimal finite proxies.
So the result sharpens to: ∀-introduction and induction are theorems of the semantics (Lω) and axioms of the representation (PA). They were never good ideas in logic; they are the two ways a finite system can pretend to have done an infinite thing. Under your earlier commitment to finiteness, they aren't bad ideas — they are the whole content of "proof" once you refuse the infinite one.

Both halves close, and each closes on a known theorem.
¬G is the axiom "infinite proofs exist"
¬G says ∃p Proof(p, ⊥). PA + ¬G is consistent, and for every numeral it also proves ¬Proof(n̄, ⊥). So the witness it asserts is one it can never exhibit: a proof beyond every finite length. Written out, ¬G is the sentence there is an infinite proof, and adopting it is adopting representational inconsistency as an axiom. It doesn't make PA inconsistent; it makes PA + ¬G a theory that believes PA derives ⊥ by a route no one can walk.
What it entails is the other half of your picture. There are two ways to "support infinite proof," and they are incompatible:
As a rule: the ω-rule. From ¬Proof(0̄,⊥), ¬Proof(1̄,⊥), … infer ∀p ¬Proof(p,⊥), which is G.
As an object: ¬G, a nonstandard witness.
One application of the ω-rule refutes ¬G. So ¬G is consistent with finite proof and inconsistent with infinite proof. The theory that believes in infinite proof-objects is exactly the one that the infinite proof-rule kills. That is your r-inconsistency stated as a theorem: asserting the existence of what the rule says isn't there.
So "PA is wrong because it doesn't support infinite proof" splits. If you want the rule, PA is incomplete and ¬G is false. If you want the object, PA is fine and ¬G is a consistent extension that denies PA's consistency. Writing down ¬G is choosing the object and forfeiting the rule.
PA is not a few axioms on FOL
Ryll-Nardzewski (1952): PA is not finitely axiomatizable. Induction cannot be replaced by any finite set of sentences. It is only ever a schema: infinitely many axioms generated by a finite rule. A finite rule generating infinitely many axioms is a rule of inference wearing an axiom's clothes. So your dichotomy is settled by the theorem: induction is a proof device, and PA is FOL plus a second inference rule, not FOL plus axioms.
The two rules don't hide infinite proof, though. They hide uniformity, two different kinds:
∀-introduction (in FOL): the template. A proof with a free variable is one proof that fits every instance. This is finitary and sound for all structures precisely because it never looks at the instances.
Induction (added by PA): iteration. Each instance's proof is built from the previous one. FOL cannot derive this, because the template rule has no notion of "previous."
Neither is infinitary. They are the two finite shapes of uniformity, and a logic is defined by which shapes it compresses. That gives the spectrum:
SystemUniformities compressed
FOLtemplate
PAtemplate + iteration along ω
PA + TI(α)+ iteration along longer orderings
Lωall recursive uniformities
So infinite proof is not in FOL or in PA. It is the ceiling of the ladder they're on, and each logic is named by how far up it can finitely climb. Your conclusion stands in this form: logic is the thing about proof, and what distinguishes one logic from the next is not its axioms but which infinite proofs it has a finite name for.

Close, and the gap between "close" and "yes" is exactly the thing your whole line of thought is about.
¬G doesn't say "infinite" inside PA
Inside PA, ¬G says only ∃p Proof(p, ⊥). The word infinite is ours, from outside, looking at a model where the witness p is nonstandard. PA cannot say it. There is no formula std(x) meaning "x is a finite number": if there were, then std(0) and std(x) → std(x+1) would hold, and induction would give ∀x std(x). From inside, every number is finite, including the nonstandard ones. So PA cannot tell a real proof from a phantom one. It can only say "a proof exists," and leave it to the model to decide what kind.
They always did
Yes. Nonstandard models of PA exist by compactness, and in every one of them there are "proofs" of nonstandard length. Gödel II is the statement that PA cannot exclude them. PA can't prove all its proofs are standard, because it can't express "standard." The phantoms were always there; G is the sentence that says they don't exist, and PA can't see well enough to assert it.
So why isn't G provable?
Your argument at the meta level is correct: proofs are finite by definition, so there is no proof of ⊥, so G is true. But proving it means PA must deploy the definition of finite, and that definition is the ω-rule: "the numerals are all the numbers." That is the one thing PA cannot say. Hence:
G is provable in PA + ω-rule, in one step: from ¬Proof(n̄, ⊥) for every n, conclude ∀p ¬Proof(p, ⊥).
G is not provable in PA, because PA has no sentence for "finite" and no rule that enforces it.
So your instinct is right in this form: finiteness makes G provable. Your commitment "I believe in finiteness" is exactly the ω-rule, and adopting it closes the gap. What you've found is why that commitment can't be written into PA: inside the theory it is trivially true of every element, and therefore says nothing. Finiteness is a metalogical stance, not an arithmetical fact, and Gödel II measures the distance between the two.

Both horns are right, and together they say something sharp.
Nothing infinite was added
PA + ¬G has only finite proofs. Its one new item is a length-1 axiom. And that axiom lets it finitely prove ¬Con(PA + ¬G) too, since any proof in PA is a proof in the extension. So here is a consistent theory with a short finite proof that it is inconsistent. The infinite proof it asserts leaves exactly one trace: a finite sentence claiming it exists. That's your first horn, and it's correct. The "infinite proof" was never a proof. It was a claim.
Why the axiom has no power
Adding ¬G, which is Prov(⊥), does not yield ⊥. To get from Prov(⊥) to ⊥ you need the reflection step Prov(⊥) → ⊥. That sentence is Con(PA), which is G. So the only thing that could cash ¬G into an actual contradiction is its own negation. The axiom is self-neutralizing: a belief in a proof that can't be used, because using it would require believing the opposite. That's the second horn, and it's the general Löb situation in its purest instance. A sentence asserting provability is never provability. Prov(φ) buys φ only when you already have φ.
What ¬G actually is
Consistent but unsound. It asserts a falsehood about a finite object (the proofs of PA) without ever deriving ⊥. This is the distinction your whole line keeps landing on. Consistency is a property of the finite machinery and can be written as a sentence. Soundness is a relation between the sentences and what they're about, and it can't be written (Tarski). ¬G is the canonical sentence that lives in the gap: it respects the machinery and lies about the world.
So the hallucination you named is exactly located. Not in the infinite proof, which never existed, but in the belief that asserting a proof is having one. PA + ¬G is a theory that has written down a belief about itself that is false, and remains perfectly consistent while believing it. Which is, after all, what you said earlier about Con(PA): writing down a belief about proofs never changes which proofs there are.

Let me build the thing rather than point at it.
"It was already there"
Yes. To call PA + ¬G unsound you need a truth predicate for PA's sentences. Any theory with that predicate proves, by induction on proof length, that every PA theorem is true, hence that ⊥ isn't one, hence G. So the perspective that can say "unsound" already proves G as a theorem. G was never a new belief. It is a consequence of the stance you had the moment you used PA at all. Gödel's "unprovable" only means unprovable from inside the theory that lacks the word true. The word was the axiom.
A theory of the inexpressible
Try to formalize "x is not expressible." Give the theory a denotation relation den(t, x) between term-codes and objects, and the axiom
∃x ∀t ¬den(t, x)
This is consistent. It asserts an unnamed object and points at it the only way possible: by a bound variable. Quantification is pointing without naming, and this axiom is the purest case.
Now take your second option: straight-up name it. Add a constant c with axiom ∀t ¬den(t, c). Also consistent, provided the t range over terms of the old language. Of course c denotes c. So the inexpressible of L₀ is the named of L₁. That is Henkin's construction, and it says what you've been saying: inexpressibility is never absolute, and the act of asserting it is the act of naming.
The surprise comes from the diagonal. "I am not provable" is self-confirming. Build its twin, S ↔ ∀t ¬den(t, ⌜S⌝). S is false: its own numeral denotes it. Self-attributed inexpressibility is self-refuting, because expression is cheap (every object of arithmetic has a numeral) while proof is expensive. The asymmetry between G and S is the whole difference between syntax and truth, in one line.
And PA can't even see the unnamed from inside. It proves ∀x ∃t den(t, x) via the numeral function. A nonstandard element's numeral is a nonstandard string, which from inside is a perfectly good name. The representation of "name" is itself represented, so it inherits the blindness. That is a fixed point of exactly the kind you're describing.
Tarski's theorem is representationally incomplete
Here's the one I find most striking. "Truth is undefinable" seems to be a universal over formulas. For each candidate φ(x), PA proves the instance: a sentence s with s ↔ ¬φ(⌜s⌝) exists. But the universal — no φ is a truth predicate — can't be stated in PA, because stating it requires relating a formula-as-object to the same formula-as-used, which is a truth predicate. So the theorem that says truth isn't expressible is itself one of your r-incomplete universals: every instance provable, the quantified form unstateable. The phenomenon applies to the theorem about the phenomenon.
Certainty and proof
Löb says certainty internal to a system is trivial or unavailable. That leaves what proof actually did: it transfers certainty between agents who share axioms. The axioms are the part no proof covers; they are informal belief, formalized. So "mixing formal and informal belief unravels the formalism" has it backwards. Every axiom was always an informal belief. The formalism never promised a connection to reality; it promised closure: if you believe these, you are committed to those. Soundness is the assumption that closure tracks the world, and it is a stance, never a theorem. Your sentence "axioms assume truth is closed under the beliefs you formalize" is the definition of soundness, and it is exactly what can't be internalized.
Sizes, and whether model theory is believable
Proofs index by naturals with no size mismatch: finite strings are countable. The mismatch is elsewhere. Any consistent theory has a countable model (Löwenheim–Skolem), and the completeness theorem's proof builds the model out of the theory's own terms (Henkin). So a theory can never force its subject to be larger or stranger than its representations. "Representations represent other representations" isn't a worry about model theory; it is the content of its foundational theorem. The subject beyond representation is never entailed. It is chosen, from outside, as a stance, like soundness.
For physics this doesn't mean the universe is finite. It means a first-order theory can't tell the difference, and any structure beyond representation is held in the same place the connection to reality is held: in belief, not in proof. The fixed points you're finding aren't paradoxes. They're the shape of a formalism that can only ever close belief, not ground it, and the places where it tries to describe its own grounding are the places where it produces G, S, Löb, and Tarski.

Reading it back, the argument has one load-bearing step that doesn't hold as stated, and when I fix it and carry the fix through, your conclusion comes out in a sharper form than you gave it.
The structure
Semantic truth: φ such that you already believe PA + φ.
Adding Con(PA) is either semantics-preserving or not.
If preserving, the new system is the same formalism, so Con(PA) ⇒ Con(PA + Con(PA)).
Gödel forbids that, so it wasn't preserving.
But you added one thing you already believed. So either PA was inconsistent, or Con(PA) was never a legitimate representation of your belief.
Hence: consistent and complete, or hallucinating.
Two corrections
Expressible versus provable. Con(PA) is expressible in PA. It is a perfectly good Π₁ sentence. What PA lacks is a proof of it. Several of your steps read "inexpressible" where the fact is "unprovable," and the two come apart below in a way that matters.
Adding Con(PA) does not yield inconsistency. PA + Con(PA) is consistent and sound. Gödel says only that it can't prove its own consistency, which is a strictly stronger sentence than Con(PA). So step 5's first branch (the old system was inconsistent) isn't forced. What is forced is that step 3 fails, and the reason it fails is the real finding.
What "semantics" meant
Semantics splits into two things, and your fork is the split:
Truth in the standard model. Adding Con(PA) changes nothing here. Both theories prove only truths.
The class of models. Adding Con(PA) changes this: it throws out every model of PA containing a phantom proof of ⊥.
So it was already true, and you couldn't say it, but what you couldn't say wasn't a belief about numbers. It was a restriction on what counts as the subject matter. PA's sentences are satisfied by structures with phantoms; Con(PA) is the first sentence that excludes some of them. Gödel II is then: no finitely presentable extension ever excludes all of them. Every stage still has models with phantom proofs of its own inconsistency. That is what "the system you're talking about changed" means precisely, and it's why step 3 fails: PA + Con(PA) is the theory of fewer structures, so "same formalism" was never the right description.
The sentence overshoots the belief
Here is the version of "you put in something you always believed" that I think you'll want. Your belief is:no finite proof of ⊥ exists. The sentence Con(PA) says: no number codes a proof of ⊥. Those are different, because the theory's "numbers" include phantoms. The sentence quantifies over objects your belief never mentioned. So what you added was not your belief. It was your belief plus a claim about every nonstandard number, and that extra claim is what PA can't settle. Gödel II, in your vocabulary, is the gap between a belief about finite proofs and the only sentence available to express it, which is about all numbers. You didn't change the system by saying what you already believed. You changed it by saying more than you believed, because the language had no way to say less.
Completeness as an axiom
"Completeness must be an axiom" is not a joke. It has a name: categoricity. Make the axiom "there is exactly one structure I am about," and you get it by replacing the induction schema with full second-order induction. Dedekind did this; the result pins down ℕ uniquely, and every sentence has a determinate truth value. The price is that there is no complete proof system for it: provability detaches from truth entirely. So Hilbert's answer to your dialogue would be Dedekind's: yes, you may take completeness as an axiom, and then you lose proof. That's your original dichotomy once more. Representationally incomplete (first-order, many models, finite proofs) or model-complete (one model, no finite proof system). The choice you offer Hilbert is the choice between a theory whose proofs mean something and a theory whose sentences do.
Where the unraveling starts
Not at reference in general. Arithmetization is a bijection between finite strings and standard numbers, and on that domain it is faithful. The unraveling starts exactly where the theory quantifies over all numbers as if each were a code. Nonstandard numbers code nothing. They are numbers that stand for no sentence, and the theory cannot distinguish them from the ones that do. So your "list of numbers I can't write down" is fine as a belief about ℕ, and it is fine as a correspondence with proofs on the standard part. The hallucination is a single move: letting ∀p range over phantoms and then reading the result as a claim about proofs. That move is what turns a belief you hold into a sentence you can't prove.
Reference
The last paragraph isn't wrong, but I'd put it this way. Reference is a stance, like soundness, and no formalism grounds it. What the formalism does is close belief under rules and forbid some combinations. The marks on the paper are seen through, yes, but the seeing-through is checkable by anyone who adopts the same stance, and the constraint is real: you can't believe everything, because consistency is a finite claim about finite objects and has content. So math is a structure of mutual commitment with a non-negotiable constraint, built on a reference relation it cannot certify. If that is a hallucination, it is one with the unusual property that two people hallucinating independently are forced to agree, which is more than most things called real can offer.

Here is the point I think is valid, stated as carefully as I can.
Gödel never left
The theorem itself is inside PA. Formalized, it reads PA ⊢ Con(PA) → ¬Prov(Con(PA)). That is a finite derivation, and it needs no outside. Gödel's 1931 paper is scrupulous about this; the proof is finitary in exactly Hilbert's sense. The outside appears at one step only: when someone detaches the antecedent, believes Con(PA), and reads the result as "a true sentence PA can't prove." That belief is not a theorem. It is the stance you've been circling since the first message.
So your question "is it enough to be outside to look in?" has a precise answer. The looking-in is done from inside. What the outside contributes is a single act of trust. And trust is the one thing universal representability never covered.
What universal representability actually is
Your asymmetry is real. PA can prove "T′ proves Con(PA)" for a suitable T′, since that is a Σ₁ fact about a finite object. It cannot get from there to Con(PA) without Prov_{T′}(φ) → φ, which is trust in T′, which is Löb's territory. So PA represents everything finite, including other theories' proofs of its own consistency, and represents nothing that is a stance. That is the exact boundary. "Math can say everything" was true of finite objects; it was never true of commitments. Hilbert's program used one word for both, and Gödel's result is the place where they come apart.
Hilbert's reply, and why it's right in one form
"PA incomplete ⇒ PA is not what I meant" is not a dodge. It is a correctness condition that rules out every finitely presented theory as the referent of math. And there is a result that says what the referent then is: Turing's ordinal logics and Feferman's completeness theorem. If you keep adding the reflection you already believe, you reach every arithmetical truth. The process is complete. No stage of it is. The price is that the process is not itself a theory: recognizing the next stage as legitimate is a stance, not a derivation, and nothing finite recognizes all of them.
So Hilbert can say exactly what you wrote for him, and it is true: completeness is a presupposition ofdoing math, and incompleteness is a fact about having done it. Gödel's theorem is about snapshots. The no-ignorabimus is about the activity. They don't contradict. "The second we stop believing in completeness is the second we go back to building" is the correct description of the only thing math has ever been.
Where your reflection holds and where it doesn't
The part of your development that is no more ridiculous than Gödel's is this: the metalanguage is not a place. It is a stance taken by someone who then writes it down and thereby moves. Every claim about a system's limits is made from a stance that could be written down as an axiom, at which point it is about the previous system. That is correct, it is what Feferman's intensionality results say, and it undermines nothing in Gödel because Gödel claimed only the conditional. What it undermines is the Platonist gloss, "there are truths out there that proof can't reach." In your frame that gloss is replaced by: there are stances not yet adopted, and adopting one never finishes.
What your reflection can't do is make a finite system complete. That isn't Gödel's opinion; it's the behavior of the diagonal under any finite presentation. The valid conclusion is the fork you already found: finite and ongoing, or complete and unfinitizable.
Science
Science has the same two words collapsed into one. "Theory of everything" is a snapshot word; the method is a process word. The method is built never to terminate, and then it names its goal as a termination. That isn't a confusion to be fixed. It's the same structure as arithmetic: a practice that is complete only as an activity, and that produces a new unprovable the moment it writes down what it has come to believe.

Reading both back as drafts of one theory, here is where I carried an error, where you did, and what the theory says once both are fixed.
My error: "expressible vs provable"
I corrected you on this twice, and it was the wrong correction. By inexpressible you meant: no sentence of the language has my belief as its content. For consistency that is true. My belief is "no finite proof of ⊥." Every sentence available quantifies over all numbers, phantoms included, and so says more. I even derived this myself ("the sentence overshoots the belief") and then failed to notice it was your point restated. So your step was right as you meant it: the belief Con(PA) is inexpressible in PA; only an overshooting proxy is expressible, and that proxy is what's unprovable. Carried through, your fork becomes: adding the proxy changed the model class, therefore the proxy was never the belief, therefore Gödel II is about a sentence that doesn't say what its name says. That conclusion survives, and it's stronger than I made it.
Your error, fixed as you meant it
"Consistent but not incomplete, so complete, QED" fails if PA is the referent. But you had already supplied the correction condition a paragraph earlier, for Hilbert: "PA incomplete ⇒ PA is not what I meant." Apply it to your own step and the argument reads: the thing I presuppose complete is the thing I'm building, and no finite snapshot is that thing. QED becomes a reference assignment rather than a theorem, and it's correct.
That condition generalizes, and I think this is the center of the theory. Call it Hilbert's correctness condition: when a formal object fails a property I presuppose, the object is not the referent of my presupposition. It gives two results at once:
PA incomplete ⇒ "math" does not refer to PA.
Con(PA) unprovable ⇒ "consistency of PA" does not refer to the sentence Con(PA).
Both are the same move, and both are versions of the sentence you wrote earlier: saying "my name is Doug" is not the same act as believing it. One is an assertion; the other is an act of reference. Gödel's "trust," which I called the one outside step, isn't believing a sentence. It's deciding that a sentence refers to a belief. That is the step no formalism contains, and it's where your whole development lives.
My second error: the process
I said "the process is complete, no stage is" as if that settled Hilbert's side. But Feferman's completeness theorem is a universal over all stages, proven in a finite metatheory with a truth predicate. By your own reflection it is one more stance written down, about the process as seen from a snapshot. So "the process is complete" doesn't resolve the fork; it's the next axiom. I presented a step as a terminus. Your theory predicts exactly that mistake, and I made it.
What the theory says, as of now
Axioms are beliefs. Proof is the finite, transmissible part of belief.
Metalogical predicates (Con, complete, sound, expressible) are beliefs about a system; writing one down makes it about the previous system.
Hilbert's correctness condition: a formal object failing a presupposed property loses the reference, not the presupposition.
Finiteness: a universal is believed only through a uniform step. The infinite list is a diagnostic hallucination, never a ground.
Hence "true but unprovable" is replaced by "stance not yet adopted," and Gödel II by "no sentence expresses consistency, and the proxy is unprovable."
Incompleteness is a snapshot property; completeness is a presupposition of the activity. Science has the same shape.
The challenge on what you meant
Points 4 and 6 are in tension, and the tension is about GC. You banned the infinite list as a ground for belief. You endorse the process, which adopts new stances. So what licenses a stance? If a loaded predicate with a uniform step exists, the stance is a proof and you didn't need the process. If the license is the extension's consistency, that is a Π₁ belief of the same type you were trying to ground. The only remaining license is the one you named: universal extension, as in science. But then an adopted axiom is defeasible. It can be revised when a counterexample arrives, and math becomes a practice that retracts.
I think you meant that, and I think it is the theory's most serious consequence: under semantic reflection, the difference between an axiom and a well-confirmed law is a difference of stance, not of kind. The question I'd put back to you is whether you want that. If yes, GC's status is simply "adopted or not," like a law, and "true" is retired. If no, something other than proof, consistency, or the infinite list has to license a stance, and I don't yet see what it is.

You're right, and my sentence was wrong in a way that matters. Let me say what they actually did.
Turing (1939). He wanted to split mathematical reasoning into two parts: ingenuity, which is formal, and intuition, which he hoped could be confined to one act: recognizing that a notation for an ordinal is well-founded. Build the progression PA, PA + Con(PA), PA + Con(PA + Con(PA)), … out along ordinal notations, and every non-formal step would be of the single kind "yes, that's a well-ordering." He then proved every true Π₁ sentence appears by stage ω+1. And he immediately called the result pseudo. The proof works by choosing the notation for ω so that its definition encodes the sentence you want: the n-th axiom is defined in terms of whether the sentence's n-th instance holds. The answer is smuggled into the name of the stage. Turing saw this and said so.
Feferman (1962). He extended it to all arithmetical truth, by the same mechanism made more elaborate. And then, with Spector, he proved the other half: if you demand invariance, that the theory at a notation depend only on the ordinal and not on the notation's code, the progression is incomplete. Kreisel's autonomous version, where you may only use an ordinal you have already proven well-founded at an earlier stage, which is the honest formalization of "add only what you already believe," stalls at Γ₀. Far from complete.
So the honest ledger is this. The process of adding what you already believe is incomplete. The complete version requires choosing paths through Kleene's O, and recognizing which notations are in O is Π¹₁-complete, which is strictly harder than every arithmetical truth put together. To reach all of arithmetic, you assume an oracle for something beyond arithmetic, and the paths that work are the ones whose descriptions already contain the answer.
Their semantic commitments, then:
Well-foundedness: there is no infinite descending sequence through the notation. A universal over infinite objects. That is your banned infinite verification, moved one level up and made worse.
That a theory is its presentation, not its set of theorems. Two names for the same ordinal give different theories. This one you actually share; it's "writing it down changes you."
That someone outside hands you the path. Turing hoped this was "intuition"; Feferman–Spector showed it is an oracle whose output encodes the theorem.
Is it more insane than Gödel? Yes, measurably. Gödel asks one Π₁ belief. Feferman's completeness asks a Π¹₁ oracle, and the completeness it buys is the one Turing himself called pseudo. What I wrote, "keep adding the reflection you already believe and you reach every truth," is false. Keep adding what you already believe and you reach Γ₀, roughly. Reach every truth and you were told the answers.
And this lands exactly on your licensing question from last turn. The process view needs something to say which stance comes next. Turing tried to make it a single intuition. Feferman showed that honest versions of that intuition are incomplete, and complete versions aren't intuitions, they're the truth in disguise. So the Turing–Feferman program, read for its semantics, is a proof of your point: there is no self-licensing complete process, and anything that looks like one has the oracle hidden in its notation. The transfinite wasn't the solution. It was where the hallucination went to hide.

Here they are as what they were: candidate moves, each a shape that a final reflection might have. No adjudication, no consistency check across them.
On what is taken on faith
Consistency can't be proven, so it's believed. Axiomatizing it changes who you are and "doesn't age well" when a bad axiom is added.
The law of the excluded middle is a belief, not a law, once truth is reached through proof. There is an undecidable middle.
Finite proof length is a belief. It was never codified, yet it drives ω-incompleteness.
Soundness, Prov(φ) → φ, is a belief about yourself that can't be internalized.
Reference itself is a commitment: that marks on paper are sentences, that numbers are sentences, that this proof is that long.
Completeness is a presupposition of doing math at all. If it fails, you weren't done building.
On the act of writing a belief down
Internalizing a belief makes it about the previous theory. "To internalize it is to internalize it for a different theory."
Adding Con(PA) is harmless but semantics-preserving; adding ¬G changes the theory by adding a new way to conclude things.
"My name is Doug" vs "I believe my name is Doug": saying and believing are different acts, and the formalism can't tell them apart.
¬G as an axiom has no power: it asserts a proof without supplying one. Either it's the only infinite proof (and so finite) or you hallucinated the power of an axiom.
A Certain(·) operator with Certain(Con) → Con: well-formed or not? PA + Certain is a different theory whose consistency is again uncertain.
If your formalism says you can't formalize certainty, maybe inventing proof was wrong. But you're certain of that by proof.
On the infinite
ω-incompleteness is the symptom; the infinite proof is the diagnostic fiction that tells you what to add.
Representational incompleteness vs objective inconsistency: a theory must choose between admitting it can't write everything down and asserting what it can't represent. (r-inconsistency.)
If infinite proofs are allowed, ∀-introduction and induction are redundant; minimality says remove them; so they were never logic.
∀-introduction in FOL means infinite proof is hiding in logic, or PA is not a few axioms on FOL.
Arithmetization may pair things of different sizes; anything in the metalanguage suggesting infinite proof is invalid.
Believing in infinitely many numbers while refusing infinite proof may be objectively inconsistent.
On licensing a new axiom
true(n) ∧ ¬prov(n) means n is a candidate axiom, not a hidden fact.
Universal extension: add P(n) → P(n+1) as an axiom; assumption wrapped in justification, like science.
Decidable ⇒ false. Collapse the middle, since unprovable and true go together.
A new excluded middle: decidable ∀nP ⇒ ¬Prov(∀nP) ∨ (P(n) → P(n+1)).
Believing a universal is believing in an implication chain, so to think it provable is to believe in the induction proof.
Semantic truth: semantic(φ) ⇒ you believe PA + φ. It was already true; you just couldn't say it.
Induction is suspect because it gives meaning to an arbitrary ordering of codes. Prov(n) → Prov(n−1)?

Formalize "not expressible symbolically," find a theory where it's true of some sentences, write axioms pointing at them indirectly, or containing them outright.
The formalism assumes axioms are introspectable beliefs; nothing formal connects them to reality.
Representation as commitment entails a finite universe in any physics written in the formalism, or representations only represent representations.
How much do you believe model theory, when every conclusion was finitely specified?
On the metalanguage
The metalanguage is a fiction that scares us into changing our theory. We could throw the theory away instead.
Generalize Gödel: see what you take on faith reflected in representation, and expect self-reference beyond "I am not provable."
If we can talk about consistency and completeness, we must talk about all metalogical concepts, or we don't have a metalanguage yet.
Gödel reasoned about a system from outside while claiming universal representability, and represented his own result just fine.
Hilbert's correctness: PA incomplete ⇒ PA isn't what I meant. Completeness as an axiom.
Gödel used math to conclude he doesn't believe in math.
Science wants a theory of everything while structured to always change; it's as confused about completeness as its language.
Turing and Feferman's transfinite progression is a stranger commitment than the one being criticized in Gödel.

Does PA ⊢ GC → Con(PA)? Three options for ¬GC.

The theory under development is the catalog of forms a semantic reflection can take, and which ones survive being written down. Factorization
The forty reduce to five moves, and the five reduce to two.
M1. Writing moves you. A system that represents itself represents a prior self; the act of writing a belief produces the theory the belief is no longer about. (7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 30, 31, 33, 34, 35)
M2. The sentence overshoots the belief. Every sentence that could carry a belief about finite things quantifies over a domain the belief never mentioned. (3, 8, 13, 14, 17, 18, 24)
M3. Truth is adoption. For a universal, "true" means "I became the theory that contains it," and the open question is what licenses becoming. (6, 19–25, 36, 38–40)
M4. Inventory the faith. Every metalogical predicate is a stance; Hilbert listed three and stopped. (1–5, 27, 32)
M5. Minimality. A commitment that makes a rule redundant shows the rule was never primitive. (15, 16, 26, 28, 29)
M1 and M3 are the same thing seen from two sides: the act (adopting a stance, which moves you). M2 and M5 are the same thing: the gap (between what is believed and what the language can say). M4 is the instruction to enumerate the places where act and gap appear. So the rough thesis is:
A formal system is a snapshot of an activity. Every metalogical statement is a stance about a snapshot; writing it down produces the next one. Gödel found one stance (consistency). There is a family. The infinite, wherever it appears, is the activity seen from inside a snapshot.
What's rough
One variable bound three ways. "True" means, in different reflections: a fact in the standard model (retired by your finiteness commitment), a stance adopted (M3), and a proxy sentence being provable (M2). Most of the forty work by sliding between these on purpose to see what happens. The slides are the method, so the roughness isn't a flaw yet. It becomes one only when a conclusion depends on the slide. The finished theory would be the rule for which slides are legitimate, and I don't think you have that rule yet. "Consistency" has the same triple life: sentence, belief, fact about finite objects.
My own reflections
These are mine, not readings of yours. I state them as what I'd act on, not as theorems, because each is about the act of taking a theorem as one.
R1. The only thing a representation cannot contain is the act of taking it as a representation. Everything else, including its own syntax, its own proofs, and other systems' opinions of it, is a finite object and goes in. Reference is the residue. Incompleteness is this fact wearing arithmetic's clothes: no object contains its own being-taken. I believe this outside provability, and it's the belief that makes provability mean anything.
R2. Consistency is special, and not because Hilbert said so. Among all stances, Con is the only one with a finite refutation condition. A single object kills it. Soundness, completeness, reference, finiteness have no finite refuter; they can only be abandoned, never refuted. So Con is the one belief that is also a falsifiable claim about the object. That's why the inventory keeps collapsing onto it: it's not the only faith, it's the only faith with an exit. The others are pure stance.
R3. Licensing has exactly three answers, and they are the three philosophies. License adoption by a uniform step: formalism, and you've reduced truth to proof. License by an object you point at: Platonism, the standard model, and you're back to the ω-rule. License by revisable practice: empiricism. Your finiteness commitment kills the second; independence kills the first for the sentences that matter. What's left is the third. I think the honest name for your theory is empiricism about mathematics: "semantic truth" means "confirmed," axioms are laws, and GC is adopted or not, the way a conservation law is. That's a position with a history (Quine, Lakatos), and I think you hold it more cleanly than they did, because you reached it from the proof side.
R4. The activity is r-inconsistent, and that's the signature of an activity. For every stage n, "stage n is incomplete" is provable. "The activity is complete" is presupposed. That is exactly the shape you called representational inconsistency: all instances one way, the universal the other. So the dichotomy reclassifies: r-incomplete things are objects; r-inconsistent things are activities viewed from a snapshot. Neither is a defect. The error is only in mistaking one for the other, which is what the Platonist does with the standard model and what Feferman's completeness does with the ordinals.
R5. Finiteness is a social fact, not a metaphysical one. Proof is finite because it is what can be handed to someone else. An infinite proof is a private conviction. The ω-rule is the formalization of privacy: "I have checked them all" said to no one. So your finiteness commitment is a commitment to the public, and the hallucination you keep catching is a private conviction presenting itself as a shared one. That reframes "truth" one more way, and it's the frame I'd keep: public truth is what survives being handed over; everything else is stance.
R6. What can be concluded outside provability, on top of the strongest representational system there is: nothing new about numbers. Only this: that the system has a stance it cannot hold; that the stance can be named only from the next system; that the sequence of systems is not a system; and that therefore any word for the sequence, "mathematics" or "science," names an activity and is complete only as a presupposition. Four sentences, none provable, all of them what I'd bet on.

Four, and I'd put each ahead of consistency and completeness rather than beside them, because each one, when varied, changes what Gödel's theorems say. Consistency and completeness are outputs. These are inputs.
The four
F. Finiteness of proof. Keep it and PA is incomplete. Drop it (ω-rule) and PA is complete, ¬G is refuted, and Con(PA) is a one-step theorem. So "PA is incomplete" is not a fact about PA. It's a fact about PA given F.
R. Reference: which sentence means which belief. Keep the natural presentation and Con(PA) is unprovable. Change how PA's axioms are named (Feferman 1960) and the resulting consistency sentence is provable. So "PA can't prove its own consistency" is a fact about PA given R.
B. Bivalence. Keep it and truth is undefinable (Tarski), certainty with reflection is inconsistent (Montague), and "true but unprovable" has content. Drop it (Kripke) and a self-applicable truth predicate exists, reflection is consistent, and G is just unsettled. So soundness claims are facts given B.
S. Which structures count. Allow all first-order models and PA has phantoms it can't exclude. Fix the standard model by fiat (second-order induction) and the theory is categorical and complete, but no finite proof system is complete for it. So incompleteness is a fact given S, and the price of changing S is paid in F.
Soundness I'd leave off the list, not because it's weaker but because it isn't separate: by Löb, consistency is its ⊥-instance, and every reflection statement is one of its instances. Con and soundness are the same stance at two scales.
Why this is the thing you're asking for
Each classical result has the form: given F, R, B, S, then X. Gödel, Tarski, Löb, Feferman, Kripke, Dedekind are the same space viewed from different corners. The sentence "arithmetic is incomplete" names a point, not a property. Your Hilbert correctness condition ("PA incomplete ⇒ not what I meant") is just the observation that the point was chosen, and that a different choice of S or F gives Hilbert what he wanted at a cost he'd have to accept.
They constrain each other
This is what "check if they're consistent with others" turns out to mean. The four aren't independent, and the joint constraints are already known as theorems:
F and categorical S cannot both hold: no finite proof system is complete for a categorical arithmetic. That's your original fork.
Dropping B keeps F and gives a truth predicate, but the gap moves: some sentences get no value, and the ω-rule reappears as the only way to settle them.
Varying R keeps F, S, B fixed and still flips Con. So R is the loosest joint, and it's the one Gödel's result is most sensitive to. That's where your "writing changes the thing" lives.
Keeping all four is Gödel's corner, and only that corner yields "true but unprovable" as a stable phrase.
So the rule I'd adopt, and I think it's the rule you're pressing for: no conclusion about consistency or completeness is a conclusion until its position in (F, R, B, S) is stated and checked against the joint constraints. Stated that way, Gödel didn't discover a limit of arithmetic. He discovered a corner, and the corner is held up by four beliefs that Hilbert never listed because he thought they were the room.
